enonce_markdown:
Read the sentence below, then choose the connector that correctly completes it.

> Emmanuel stayed at home ___ he was feeling very sick.
corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode

To find a connector of cause, ask which part of the sentence gives the reason for the fact stated in the other part. 'Because' (like 'since' and 'as') introduces the reason for what happens; it must not be confused with 'so', which introduces the result of that reason, not the reason itself.

### Corrigé

In this sentence, staying at home is the result, and feeling very sick is the reason for that result. The connector must therefore introduce the reason, which is exactly the role of 'because'. The correct answer is **A) because**. Option B ('so') would reverse the logic, since 'so' introduces a result, not a reason: 'Emmanuel stayed home so he was feeling sick' would wrongly suggest that staying home caused the illness. Option C ('although') would signal a contrast between the two facts, but there is no contrast here: feeling sick and staying home are not opposed, one simply explains the other. Option D ('otherwise') introduces an unwanted alternative that would happen if a condition were not met, which has no place in this simple cause-and-effect sentence.

enonce_markdown:
Read the sentence below, then choose the connector that correctly completes it.

> The teacher explained the lesson twice, ___ every student finally understood it.
corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode

To find a connector of consequence, look for the connector that introduces the result of a fact already stated, after that fact has been presented. 'So' (like 'therefore' and 'thus') introduces this result; it must never be confused with 'because', which introduces the cause of a result that appears later in the sentence.

### Corrigé

Here, the teacher explaining the lesson twice is the fact, and every student understanding it is the result of that fact. The connector must therefore introduce a result, which is exactly what 'so' does. The correct answer is **B) so**. Option A ('because') would reverse the order of cause and result, producing an illogical sentence, as if the students' understanding were the reason the teacher explained the lesson twice. Option C ('unless') introduces a condition under which something would not happen, which does not fit a sentence describing something that did happen. Option D ('however') would introduce a contrast, but there is no contrast between explaining a lesson twice and students finally understanding it: the second fact follows naturally from the first, it does not oppose it.

enonce_markdown:
Read the sentence below, then choose the word that correctly completes it.

> ___ Sandrine had studied very hard for the test, she did not get a good mark.
corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode

To identify a connector of concession, check whether the second part of the sentence contradicts what would normally be expected from the first part. 'Although' (like 'though' and 'even though') introduces a fact that does not prevent the main clause from happening, unlike 'because', which would present that same fact as the reason for what follows.

### Corrigé

Studying very hard would normally be expected to lead to a good mark, yet Sandrine did not get one: the two parts of the sentence are in tension with each other, which is exactly what a connector of concession signals. The correct answer is **A) Although**. Option B ('Because') would present hard studying as the reason for the bad mark, which is not a logical cause-and-effect relationship, since studying hard does not cause a bad result. Option C ('So') cannot introduce a subordinate clause placed before the main clause in this way: it links a result to a cause already stated, and does not work as a sentence opener followed by a comma and a full clause. Option D ('Unless') would introduce a condition ('if Sandrine had not studied hard'), which does not match a sentence reporting what actually happened.

enonce_markdown:
Read the sentence below, then choose the connector that correctly completes it.

> You will fail the exam ___ you revise your lessons regularly.
corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode

To find a connector of condition expressing a negative idea, look for the word that means 'if...not'. 'Unless' introduces the only condition under which the negative outcome announced in the main clause can be avoided; it must not be confused with 'although', which presents a fact that does not change the outcome at all.

### Corrigé

'Unless you revise your lessons regularly' means 'if you do not revise your lessons regularly', so the sentence states that failing the exam can only be avoided by revising regularly. The correct answer is **B) unless**. Option A ('so') would introduce a result caused by revising, which is not the relationship intended here. Option C ('although') would mean that revising regularly does not change the outcome, contradicting the intended warning that revising is precisely what prevents failure. Option D ('moreover') simply adds an extra fact and cannot introduce a condition at all: it does not fit grammatically or logically in this sentence.

enonce_markdown:
Read the sentence below, then choose the connector that correctly completes it.

> Submit your assignment before Friday; ___, you will lose ten marks.
corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode

'Otherwise' introduces the unwanted consequence that will occur only if an instruction or condition already given is not respected; it is different from 'because'/'since', which explain a cause already realised, and from connectors of concession such as 'although'. Because 'otherwise' links two independent clauses, it must be preceded by a semicolon (or a full stop) and followed by a comma, exactly as in this sentence.

### Corrigé

The first clause gives an instruction (submit the assignment before Friday); the second clause states the negative consequence that follows only if that instruction is not respected. This is precisely the function of 'otherwise'. The correct answer is **B) otherwise**. Option A ('because') would present the loss of marks as the cause of submitting the assignment, which reverses the intended warning. Option C ('since') has the same problem as 'because': it introduces a cause, not an avoided consequence. Option D ('although') would signal a contrast between submitting the assignment and losing marks, which does not match the intended meaning of a warning about what happens if the instruction is ignored.

enonce_markdown: Read the four sentences below, then choose the one in which the logical connector is used correctly, both grammatically and logically.
corrige_markdown:
### Rappel de méthode

'Moreover' and 'furthermore' are sentence adverbs of addition, not conjunctions: when they link two independent clauses, they must be preceded by a semicolon (or a full stop) and followed by a comma, exactly like 'however'. Two connectors must never be combined to link the same pair of clauses. Semantically, 'moreover'/'furthermore' add a fact that reinforces or extends the first idea in the same direction, while 'however' introduces a contrast: the two are not interchangeable, even when the punctuation around them is correct.

### Corrigé

Both facts in this sentence point in the same direction: building classrooms and recruiting teachers are two actions that reinforce the same effort to reduce overcrowding, so the connector needed is one of addition, and it must be punctuated as a sentence adverb. The correct answer is **C**. Option A uses the right connector ('moreover') but the wrong punctuation: a comma alone before a sentence adverb linking two independent clauses creates a comma splice, whereas a semicolon (or a full stop) is required. Option B is correctly punctuated but uses the wrong connector: 'however' signals a contrast, yet recruiting teachers does not contradict or oppose building classrooms, it adds to the same effort, so 'however' misrepresents the relationship between the two facts. Option D combines two connectors ('so' and 'moreover') to link the same two clauses, which is never grammatically acceptable, and produces an incoherent, unreadable sentence.

choix.texte: The government built ten new classrooms in the school, moreover it recruited fifteen additional teachers to reduce overcrowding.
The government built ten new classrooms in the school; however, it recruited fifteen additional teachers to reduce overcrowding.
The government built ten new classrooms in the school; moreover, it recruited fifteen additional teachers to reduce overcrowding.
The government built ten new classrooms in the school so moreover it recruited fifteen additional teachers to reduce overcrowding.
